Key Takeaways & Strategic Implications

  • Temporal skew is structural, not cyclical. 80.3% of indexed abstracts originate from 2024, reflecting PubMed's inherent indexing lag. Policy analysts should treat 2025-2026 volumes as incomplete snapshots and avoid direct year-on-year count comparisons without normalization.
  • Open access momentum accelerated in 2025. The OA rate rose from 64.1% in 2024 to 74.1% in 2025 - a +10.0 percentage-point jump. However, the 2026 partial-year rate (53.8%) is artificially depressed by small-sample volatility (n=225). Funders should anticipate sustained OA pressure and plan APC budgets accordingly.
  • China dominates volume but lags on open access. China contributes 22.9% of all abstracts yet achieves only 54.7% OA - the lowest among top-10 countries. This signals a policy gap that could affect global knowledge-equity initiatives and collaborative funding frameworks.
  • COVID-19 research is declining; mental health and neuro topics are accelerating. COVID-19 dropped 28.1% in normalized share from 2024 to 2025. Conversely, Stress Disorders (Post-Traumatic) and Electroencephalography showed the strongest normalized growth (+255% and +166%, respectively), suggesting a pivot toward mental-health and neuroscience funding priorities.
  • Collaboration intensity varies sharply by geography and topic. Italy and China show the highest median author counts (8.0 and 7.0), while Quality-of-Life and Coleoptera studies cluster at the low end (4.0 and 3.5). Cancer and microbiome topics attract larger teams, indicating higher resource requirements.

Publication Volume & Temporal Distribution

The dataset spans 4,886 biomedical abstracts indexed in PubMed between January 2024 and March 2026. The temporal distribution is heavily skewed toward 2024 (3,924 abstracts, 80.3%), with progressively smaller cohorts in 2025 (737, 15.1%) and 2026 (225, 4.6%). This pattern is consistent with PubMed's indexing pipeline, where older publications have had more time to be captured and curated.

Data Quality Note: 754 records (15.4%) have unknown publication months. Monthly trend analyses below reflect only the 4,132 records with known months.

Among records with known months, January stands out as an outlier across all three years - 1,746 total January publications versus a monthly average of ~376. This is partly an artifact of default dating (many journals assign "January" to early-online articles) and partly reflects genuine Q1 publishing surges. Excluding January, the data shows a relatively flat monthly profile with modest seasonality.

Strategic Insight: The steep drop-off after 2024 is expected and should not be interpreted as a decline in global biomedical output. For forward-looking planning, analysts should model 2025 and 2026 as incomplete and apply indexing-lag correction factors when projecting full-year volumes.

Geographic Landscape of Biomedical Research

Biomedical research output in this dataset is geographically concentrated: the top 10 identifiable countries account for 51.4% of all abstracts. China leads decisively with 1,121 publications (22.9%), followed by the USA (539, 11.0%) and India (196, 4.0%).

The relative country rankings remain stable across 2024-2026, with China, USA, and India holding the top three positions in every year. However, the proportional contributions shift slightly: China's share of the known 2026 cohort is 19.6% (44/225), down from 22.9% overall, while the USA holds steady at ~11%. These shifts are within the margin of error given small 2026 sample sizes.

Collaboration Intensity by Geography

Median author count varies meaningfully by country. Italy leads with 8.0 median authors per paper, followed by China (7.0), Brazil (7.0), and Switzerland (7.0). The USA sits at 6.0, aligning with the global median. Higher author counts in Italy and China may reflect larger clinical consortia, multi-site trials, or national research programs that encourage broad authorship.

Research Topic & MeSH Keyword Analysis

All 4,886 records carry at least one MeSH major topic assignment. The most prevalent topics reflect a mix of persistent disease burdens (COVID-19, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's disease), oncology (breast neoplasms, hepatocellular carcinoma), and emerging methodological areas (gastrointestinal microbiome, microRNAs).

Topic Collaboration Patterns

Cancer-related topics attract the largest teams. Breast Neoplasms shows a median of 10.0 authors, Gastrointestinal Microbiome 8.5, and Carcinoma, Hepatocellular 8.0. By contrast, Quality of Life studies and Coleoptera research cluster at 4.0 and 3.5 median authors, respectively - suggesting these domains rely more on small specialized groups than on large consortia.

Open Access Adoption & Journal Landscape

Overall, 65.1% of abstracts in the dataset are flagged as open access (available via PubMed Central). The yearly trajectory shows a notable increase from 64.1% in 2024 to 74.1% in 2025, before dropping to 53.8% in the partial 2026 data. The 2025 figure is the most policy-relevant: it represents a completed year with a substantial sample (737 records) and suggests that OA adoption is genuinely accelerating.

Country-level OA rates vary dramatically. Among nations with at least 20 publications, Switzerland leads at 88.9%, followed by Iran (86.9%) and South Africa (81.8%). China is a notable outlier at the bottom of the top-10 list with 54.7% - nearly 20 percentage points below the global average. This gap has strategic implications for bilateral funding agreements and open-access mandate compliance.

The monthly OA rate series is volatile, oscillating between ~35% and ~88%. Much of this variance is driven by journal-specific effects: high-volume journals like Scientific Reports, Heliyon, and Cureus are 100% OA, while The Science of the Total Environment and Zootaxa are predominantly closed. When these journals publish heavily in a given month, the aggregate OA rate spikes.

Leading Journals

The journal landscape is dominated by broad-scope OA titles. Scientific Reports (n=82), Heliyon (n=76), and Cureus (n=69) occupy the top three positions. Conference proceedings (IEEE EMBC Annual International Conference, n=46) and preprint servers (bioRxiv, n=32) also feature prominently, reflecting the diversification of formal publication channels.

OA by Research Type

Open access penetration is near-universal for preprints (100%), case reports (85.4%), and clinical trial protocols (92.9%), but lower for systematic reviews (43.3%) and meta-analyses (50.0%). The latter categories often appear in subscription-based specialist journals with longer embargo periods, creating a structural OA gap in evidence-synthesis literature.

Research Type Distribution & Collaboration Indicators

Journal Articles dominate the corpus at 4,484 records (91.8%). Case Reports (178, 3.6%) are the second-largest category, followed by smaller cohorts of Randomized Controlled Trials, Preprints, Systematic Reviews, and Reviews. The 2025 and 2026 data show a relative increase in Case Reports (from 3.2% in 2024 to 5.0% in 2025 and 6.7% in 2026), though this may be an indexing-lag artifact - case reports are often indexed faster than complex trial manuscripts.

The median author count across all publications is 6, with a mean of 7.1 - a right-skewed distribution driven by a long tail of multi-author consortia (max: 115 authors). Clinical trial phases II and III show the highest medians (33.0 and 18.0 authors), reflecting regulatory and multi-site coordination requirements. At the other extreme, editorials and historical articles average just 2.0 authors.

Collaboration by Topic

Among topics with at least 10 publications, Breast Neoplasms commands the largest teams (median 10.0 authors), followed by Gastrointestinal Microbiome (8.5) and Carcinoma, Hepatocellular (8.0). These figures suggest that oncology and microbiome research are increasingly consortia-driven, with implications for grant administration, IP management, and data-sharing governance.

Data Limitations & Methodology Notes

This analysis is subject to several important constraints:

  • Indexing lag: The 80.3% / 15.1% / 4.6% year split is a function of PubMed curation speed, not actual global publication output. Cross-year comparisons should use normalized shares or rates, never raw counts.
  • Missing months: 15.4% of records lack month-level granularity, limiting seasonal analysis precision.
  • Country standardization: First-author affiliation data required extensive cleaning. 658 records (13.5%) remain unclassified after deduplication of variants (e.g., "PR China" to "China").
  • MeSH completeness: While all records in this cleaned dataset carry major topics, newer publications may receive additional MeSH terms in future indexing passes, slightly altering topic rankings.
  • 2026 volatility: With only 225 records covering January-March, 2026 statistics are provisional and should be treated as directional indicators only.
